review:
I remember a long time ago, there was someone talking about Anchorman, the 2004 Will Ferrell film. This critic said something like, "Yeah, Anchorman is funny, but I don't know if it's on the level of Ghostbusters, Airplane, or Planes, Trains and Automobiles."

My response to that was, "Yeah, I guess it's not as funny as three of the GREATEST comedies of the last thirty years. Good point." 

Superliminal is going to draw comparisons to Portal and The Stanley Parable. Some people say it's invalid to directly compare games in criticism because the reader isn't guaranteed to have played those. But screw that, you've at least played Portal and I got points to make.

Portal, Superliminal and The Stanley Parable are all first-person puzzle games where an announcer is a constant companion. But Superliminal is not as sharply designed or as good at training the player as Portal. (There is one puzzle that I had to look up the solution for, and the game really could've stood to train the player better for that one.) Nor is Superliminal as thoughtful or devastating as The Stanley Parable, and it's not half as funny as either of them.

But not being as good as two earnest masterpieces is no big deal. I enjoyed my few hours with Superliminal just fine and was satisfied with it. It also doesn't really get as dark as either game, which is sort of a relief. The Stanley Parable's almost relentless futility isn't for everyone. Superliminal has a lighter tone and no chance to 'lose' or 'die,' I don't think.

The asking price is a bit of a lurch, more than either Portal OR Stanley, so I would wait for a sale. Nevertheless, Superliminal is bright, beautiful, mesmerizing... and sometimes disorienting. Don't sleep on this one.

Or if you do... don't forget to wake up.

It's like Portal, with no portals.

But 10x trippier, and made my brain melt.

Buy. It.

Be warned going in that it's an extremely short game.  Less than 2 hours for a full story play-through and I couldn't really milk anything out of the cursory post-game level challenges and obligatory parkour secrets.  So if you're on a budget, even an on-sale price is a bit of a hard sell.

But as a comedy first-person puzzler of the "clearly inspired by Portal" genre, the comedy lands and the puzzle mechanics are mind-bending and neat.  But the nature of the perspective-based puzzles and the way they are particularly crafted to each situation, makes the puzzles feel less like challenging puzzles more as slapstick comedy and the fact that they acted more as a medium for a physical narrative rather than a platform for making puzzles is probably why it's so short.  So each segment is a unique hand-crafted experience rather than an escalation of the learned mechanics.  Which, hey, I think makes it worth experiencing.
The game is a masterpiece designed to melt your brain, then make you see your melted brain on the ground from the correct angle, reconstruct your brain, and then be made whole again.

I finished the game in about two hours, but they were pretty strong two hours. There's also a challenge mode that limits how many actions you can take, which I might give a shot to get some more mileage out of the game. Maybe grab it on sale (like it is right now at release), because maybe you have a harder time justifying a short game for $20.

Some of the criticisms for the game are levied toward the end, saying it turns into a "pretentious walking simulator." And while the perspective gimmicks slow down a bit near the end as the story wraps up, that section is short and leans more into imagery than the rest of the game. It's all thematically appropriate, but it's not utterly necessary and isn't super strong writing wise, so people overreact. It's harmless fat, really.

I do wish the game leaned more into combining the different gameplay elements, certain elements are isolated to specific levels and they don't converge further in for more complex puzzles in the way that something like Portal tutorializes and combines mechanics.

One of the most creative indie puzzle games in recent years

By turning the principle of perspective directly into its core gameplay mechanic, Superliminal delivers a surreal, dream experience filled with imagination. Through its inventive puzzles and clever design, the game effectively conveys its central philosophy of “thinking outside the box,” constantly challenging players to rethink their perception of reality.

While the game carries a strong Portal-like atmosphere, it does not explore its mechanics with the same depth. Many brilliant ideas are introduced only briefly before moving on, leaving little room for deeper development. With a runtime of under two hours, much of the experience relies on the novelty of new mechanics and environments, which, while engaging, ultimately feels a bit too short.

[h3]9/10[/h3]

This game feels like Portal and The Stanley Parable had a baby. It feels like a rat race through a fever dream designed by M. C. Escher. Recently updated with multiplayer, this game is a must play for anyone who wishes they could share their interest in surreal, comedic, impossible puzzle solving with other people. It's a great game and you've never played anything like it.
The closest game to a real-life therapy, Superliminal will force you to break down your mental limitations to achieve what seems impossible.

A "short" but powerful dive into the power of perception/perspective! 

The gameplay shows this with fun and stylish visual perspective puzzling. Gameplay effectively supports the narrative, regarding a "therapy" which to me mostly seems to target mental health. 

The narrative can be puzzling at first. However, in completing the game you experience the importance and power of perspective and flexibility/motion therein. Within this larger message it hits great points that are easily forgotten in real life, especially during difficult times. For example that it is okay and mostly temporary to be stuck. That without asking you receive (c)overt judgement and pressure from others regarding "proper" perspective. You are also driven towards "explosive mental overload" to reorient yourself. This may seem bad, but in my experience a process of true change is indeed fueled by some form of overwhelming pressure that cannot be otherwise coped with. And change can definitely be for the better.

The above is of course just my perspective - which may have been influenced by working as a therapist and currently being in a difficult time personally. I've seen other reviews calling the game pretentious. However, no matter if its insights are recognizable or new to you, I hope it will provide you with a similar sense of liberation.

So why not try it out and find your own perspective on the game?

When this game first came out and after received the “Most Innovative Gameplay” award on Steam (over Death Stranding), I felt a strong antipathy toward it. Perspective-based illusions never felt impressive to me (especially) in digital environments, because digital worlds don’t have fixed physical rules to begin with. Plus, other games had already explored similar ideas, and Superliminal looked like an extra layer built almost entirely around a single concept, perspective, without expanding or transforming it into something deeper. So I kept my distance from it with prejudice. In the end, I finally played it and my thoughts on these points didn’t really change. Yet the game managed to catch me from a different *angle*.

Superliminal is built around solving puzzles by manipulating perspective. Most puzzles are easy and predictable, i finished it under 2hs, which creates a lingering “what’s going to happen?” feeling. And yet precisely here, the game begins a subtle pedagogical process. Even though the puzzles are simple and quickly solved, the design gently conditions you, step by step, to internalize a way of seeing. This is where Superliminal does something unusual.

Most puzzle games teach you rules. For example, Portal teaches you how its physics and mechanics consistently work, then asks you to solve problems within that system. You learn how the world functions. Superliminal, however, does not really teach you how its system works. Instead, it conditions you. By repeatedly showing that what you see cannot be trusted, it trains a reflex, to doubt your first interpretation, to look again, to reinterpret space. It teaches not a rule, but a perceptual habit.

This is a fascinating pedagogical move. The game quietly repeats the same perceptual exercise until “looking differently” becomes automatic. At the end, it essentially says “I’ve taught you something.” This can feel a bit preachy but the way it arrives there feels sincere and thoughtfully constructed.

However, this very conditioning is also where the game’s final claim starts to lose strength. Near the end, the game tells you “You just overcame what seemed impossible by thinking outside the box.” But by that point, you have already been trained, over and over, not to trust what you see and to search for alternative perspectives. So the question becomes difficult to answer, did you really think outside the box, or did you simply apply a reflex the game carefully conditioned into you? In other words, you are not breaking the rules of the system of anything, you are following the process of things the game has been teaching you all along.

Because the system itself is loose, the physics and world logic unreliable, and the puzzles predictable, this conditioning is rarely tested in a way that creates a strong mental rupture. Unlike Magritte’s ''The Treachery of Images'' (which the game reminded me), where a stable reality makes representation clash with meaning, here everything is already flexible. There is nothing solid to crack.

Similarly, The Stanley Parable achieves the feeling of “thinking outside the box” far more effectively without ever stating it. A limited map, *seemingly* clear boundaries, and the curiosity to test them create that sensation through player action. Superliminal tends to say it rather than make you feel it.

In conclusion, Superliminal remains limited in its puzzle design and predictability, especially for players who already think ''outside of the box''. But its subtle pedagogical conditioning, and the simple yet thoughtful way it builds toward its final note, make it more interesting than I initially gave it credit for.

Putting it as simply as possible, this game is just [b]fun[/b].
I love games that embrace a more surreal nature, as it brings an additional level of intrigue to the experience. I think this is especially great for puzzle games, as the constant shifting and subversion of expectations really keeps you on your toes and keeps you engaged throughout the entire game.
When I first discovered this game I was so excited to play it, because the puzzle mechanic being perspective-based was just so unique to me. 

The premise of the game is that you are asleep at a sleep therapy clinic, experiencing dreams. This opens up a lot of possibility for the setting of the game to change and I think they utilise the premise perfectly.

I was very quick to notice on startup that it looks very well polished. For something that was made by a small team, it looks very well put together.
A little further in, the narration kicks in and you start to get a feel for what is going on here. I did find it a bit strange that the trailers for this game don’t show any of the narration at all, so in honesty I wasn’t 100% expecting it.
If i’m completely honest, I found the narrative just okay. It’s nothing amazing, and I found it a little cheesy at times. It isn’t bad, It’s just okay. I could see what they were going for, but it was a little monotone until the very end so I guess I didn’t find myself all that engaged with it.

There are two main characters, 
The “Standard Orientation Protocol”, the automated voice that leads people through their therapy. They drop a few lines that give it this “cold hearted computer” thing, but I found that I didn’t really care about this character at all.
Then there’s the narrator Dr. Glenn Pierce, who chimes in every now and then from (I assume) the real world. He talks in this very slow and calm voice which I assume mimics meditative audios and that kind of thing. I could see that this was perhaps supposed to get funnier as things progress [spoiler] and he essentially starts telling you that you’re trapped in there and your life is falling apart in this very chill way[/spoiler], but this fell a bit flat for me.

In general there was dialogue in the game that felt like it was written to be humorous that I recognised as such, but for me personally the comedy element did just fall a bit flat overall. In my head i’d think “ah, a joke” but I’m not sure I actually reacted at all. Something I did enjoy, that did make me at least smile, was finding a banana hidden in a level that bounced around and spins itself to the ground. That within itself shows i’m not above cheap/mediocre comedy, but for some unknown reason this game just didn’t really hit for me in the comedy department. It might for you, though!

Despite the above, which I know sounds extremely negative, I honestly didn’t mind feeling so neutral to the narrative because for me the artistry and creativity of this game, and the fun I was having playing through it, more than made up for it ten times over. Some of the puzzles are so creative that moving along to the next area, I couldn’t help but be a little excited for whatever might be next.
[spoiler] One part just randomly gets a little spooky for a bit and I genuinely didn’t expect to be made to jump by the cheeky lure of a door left ajar.[/spoiler]

After my first playthrough I peaked at the achievements and saw there was a lot of missed ones, one of which involved a speedrun. “Oh hell no”, I thought. There was a lot, but despite it seeming like too much work I decided to just try and get as many as possible. I won’t talk about all of them, obviously, but i’ll touch on some of them as they are content related. Some are simple and obvious, and others are a bigger task.

I first attempted the challenge mode for the associated achievement, thinking I was going to give up before long. It actually wasn’t that bad though and I found it quite fun. The challenges are along the lines of “do this level only touching something X amount of times and jumping Y amount of times”. If you enjoyed the game and want that bit of extra challenge definitely give it a go.

I then played through again looking for collectables (of which there are a LOT). I didn’t find many on my first playthrough so you have to really look for them. This part was a bit tedious, and you might find you need to peak at a guide to collect them all.
There are also fire alarms and fire extinguishers you need to interact with throughout the game for a few achievements. There is a lot of them and trying to find these gets you playing the game in a very OCD-like way. You need to check behind every door, in any corner, everywhere. I found most of these on my first playthrough because I check things really thoroughly when I play games, but It still took me accessing secret areas (near other collectables) and playing through a few times to actually find them all. They are annoying achievements, but admittedly it was very satisfying once they finally popped up.

Next, the speedrun. I was not confident with this at all, I hate speedrun achievements and this game is actually something proper speedrunners play, so I figured if it was an unattainable time for an average person I was just going to leave this game nearly completed.
The speedrun time is under 30 minutes. Completing the challenge mode actually teaches you some ways to solve puzzles efficiently, so definitely do that before any attempt.
My first try I was 3 minutes over. This kind of confirmed in my head this [i]was[/i] possible for average people. I watched a speedrun, tried again and failed by 1 minute. The third time I tried, and I got the achievement with [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3437231372]only 5 seconds to spare[/url].

Finally, I saved the achievement for playing with developer commentary for last for a more chilled out end.
There were some fun insights here. [spoiler]For example, a member of the team praises the narrator for having smashed the “mixed up” voice line (where the words are out of order but the tone of the sentence is consistent) out of the park on the first try. I genuinely assumed that was impossible to do and that they had him say sentences and spliced the “mixed up” one together from the pieces. [/spoiler] It was also interesting to hear about the game design. It of course went straight over my head, but it was interesting nonetheless. If you are interested in game design I think you’d enjoy a playthrough with the commentary.

At this point i’d played through the game so many times. I honestly thought I would be more bothered at this point by having to replay the whole thing so many times over. I would usually get bored but I think because it is a fairly fast-paced illusion/maze once you know what you’re doing, it didn’t bother me. I thought trying to 100% this game would frustrate me and be a pain but I actually found it quite rewarding. By the time I was done I was glad I did it and just thought to myself “well, that was fun!”.

I definitely recommend this game. I don’t have actual rankings, but if I did I think this game would be in the top 5 first-person puzzle games for me. If they made a sequel to this game I would most definitely play it.

Stunning visuals that will definitely remind you of The Stanley Parable, and there's something in the gameplay and storytelling winking at that too : you know this is not reality, but you're still going to explore the peculiar logic (or lack thereof) governing this place.

Most of the puzzles are pretty straightforward once you get the hang of the basic mechanic, and many leave room for some improvisation. This could get repetitive, but the game is relatively short and the visuals do make up for some of it, so it works fine in my opinion.

The only serious negative point is the whole monologue towards the end. Goodness me, [i]that[/i] we could all have lived without after such a nice game. The "narrators" are fine throughout the game, but the ending... I can say without spoilers: oof.

Anyway, it's still very much enjoyable. The devs have added challenges and achievements for speedrunners, so if that's your cup of tea you'll have that cherry on top. I do recommend this game, at the very least for the gorgeous looks and for the innovative gameplay. The music is nice too!

Every challenge boils down to, make big, make small, and/or find the right angle, which I don't find fun. 

I went in with the expectation of this being a puzzle game that uses perspective mechanics. What I got was a tech demo showcasing a bunch of cool ways to use perspective in a game and the same puzzle 50 times in a row.

Maybe you'll enjoy Superliminal, but if you're looking for a challenging puzzle game, I suggest you stay clear of this one.

A lovely little game that's both enjoyable and satisfying. Picked this up on a whim, not expecting to enjoy it as much as I did. I have a soft spot for shorter games that excel in their creativity, imagination, cleverness, and design. Superliminal fits the bill.

The comps to Portal are warranted. It's a quirky first-person puzzle game with innovative and trippy mechanics that make you constantly want to experiment, and with ominous vibes that keep you wondering what's around the next corner. I'm pretty certain if you like one, you'll like the other. I'd probably give Portal the nod in terms of story and puzzle design, but Superliminal has the edge in its beauty and its engagement. The set designs are captivating and malleable, while the "levels" don't really feel like levels, but part of a continuous experience that's hard to step away from.

If you've never played this style of game before, Superliminal's length and engaging nature make it a perfect gateway to exploring a new genre. If this style of game is already your jam, then Superliminal is a must-add to your library.
 
FINAL VERDICT: Highly Recommended

What a lot the negative reviews about the puzzle aspect about this fail to grasp, is this is not a puzzle game in the traditional sense and going into it with that expectation will of course lead to a letdown. This game isn't about pushing the human mind's capacity for problem solving cleverness to new levels. You're not going to be drip fed a steady stream of new game mechanics and increasingly complex puzzles that require you to use them all to advance forward. You're not gonna feel like a genius by the time you finish this game. In fact in some cases you might feel like a fool for struggling at certain points when the solution was painfully easy and thats really the point. 
The game is more of a lighthearted philosophical journey on introspection as well as perception. The puzzle elements really are just there to drive home the point in hindsight (after all perspective is a core game mechanic after all). The game's purpose is really to get you thinking a bit more, about yourself, how you view and interact the world around you and maybe even to question yourself on what drives you forward when the path before you is not crystal clear.

So if you're down for so game that showcases the fun and wildness perspective has as well  some chill vibes to go with some light narrative that will steadily get you thinking about yourself and maybe even will prove to be therapeutic for some people by the end, then this game will probably be a nice little treat. I say little because the game isn't very long.

I guess the last question will be, is it worth about 20 dollars? To that I'd be inclined to say no, not really. However due to its good polish and quality, I'd say 15 would be a reasonable price when paired with how short it is. So I wholeheartedly recommend this game, but on sale.

I had Superliminal on my wishlist since it came out, and I really, really wanted to love it. I did. I love puzzle games and the hook of solutions being based on your perspective sounded like a great premise- it reminded me of the obelisk puzzles in The Witness, which felt very mind-bending and rewarding.  Exploring "out of bounds" of the shiny dream facility was reminiscent of Portal when you get to peek behind the grand curtains of science to the dirty behind-the-scenes, and they did a great job on the aesthetic and atmosphere.

However, even with these similarities to two of my favourite puzzle games of all time, Superliminal fell flat.

The key to a good puzzle game is when it introduces you to a mechanic, gets you used to it and makes it harder, then pushes the mechanic beyond recognition and forces you to look at the puzzle completely differently than you've gotten used to. Superliminal barely even got to the second step. The mechanics are cool in theory but never explored to a fulfilling degree, much less pushed to their limits as one might expect of a dream world. I also had qualms with how such a small number of objects had interactions enabled that it was obvious when something was key to a puzzle- it requires no thinking to just click around until you finally happen across something you can interact with.

After completing the game, it felt like every solution was either make this object bigger, make that object smaller, or stand in this specific place to perceive things the right way. All the levels flowed into one another and were not very memorable. I want a puzzle game to make me feel stupid (and trust me, it's not that hard) but it didn't happen once. You'll end up solving puzzle after puzzle after puzzle and never getting that dopamine hit when everything finally clicks into place. It is still a game with lovely graphics, intriguing story, and top-notch atmosphere, but the actual gameplay feels quite unrealized, falling well short of its potential.

[i]Superliminal[/i] is a puzzle-based adventure game from Pillow Castle.  The main story will take players between two and four hours to complete without a guide and moderate exploration.  There is some replayability in collectibles, challenge modes, and level design.

The player controls a nameless patient of Somnascult for treatment of an disclosed anxiety-based disorder.  The patient is placed in a dream state during treatment.  As the player progresses, it becomes clear that the treatment is highly experimental, the facility is too low-budget, and the treatment is going wrong.  The player must help the patient escape their dream.

[i]Superlimial[/i] centers around a forced-perspective mechanic.  Beginning in a test-chamber structure, the player develops a basic understanding of the mechanic's rules.  The player must then expand on their understanding as they work to escape.  The mechanic expands beyond the resize-the-thing-to-use-it-as-a-ramp concept.  Objects can become "real" if certain two-dimensional plains are aligned.  In some areas, all objects are duplicated when selected.  Doorways can be used to alter the player's size.  While fairly short, the two-to-four hour initial playthrough ensures that the games mechanics do not overstay their welcome.  Puzzles are fresh, well-designed, and sufficiently varied.

Humor is a fundamental component of [i]Superliminal[/i].  Humor can come from the computerized program manager, the disembodied voice of Dr. Glenn Pierce, and a few points of unexpected nuggets found while exploring.  The humor is fairly subdued.  Unfortunately, toward the end of the game, the humor dissipates as it tries to take itself seriously.

There is simply no way not to compare [i]Superliminal[/i] with [i]Portal[/i].  It's a puzzle-based game with a novel mechanic in which the player learns to control the environment through testing chambers while being monitored by a computer and then needs to escape while humor dialog narrates.  [i]Portal[/i] does what it does better because it wasn't trying to be anything.  However, [i]Superliminal[/i] deserves to be rated on its own merits.  It is a fun experience that stretches on what a puzzle can be in a virtual world.  Fans of [i]Portal[/i] or [i]The Stanley Parable[/i] will certainly enjoy [i]Superliminal[/i].

[h1]A Major Letdown in Puzzle Design[/h1]

I recently played Superliminal, and I have to say, I was disappointed. Here’s why I think Superliminal is a very bad puzzle game.

First of all, the main mechanic of the game gets old really fast. The whole idea of changing the size of objects based on perspective is interesting at first, but it quickly becomes repetitive. Every solution seems to rely on the same trick: pick up an object, move it around to change its size, and place it somewhere to proceed. After a while, it feels like you’re just doing the same thing over and over again.

The puzzles themselves are not challenging. Once you understand the core mechanic, there’s very little variety in how you approach each puzzle. The game doesn’t offer enough new ideas or ways to use the mechanics in creative ways. Instead, it just keeps throwing the same types of puzzles at you, making the whole experience feel tedious and uninspired. This lack of diversity in puzzle design makes the game feel very repetitive and uninteresting.

Another big problem is the narration and story throughout the game. While there is an attempt to have a narrative and some sort of deeper meaning, it all comes across as very meaningless and bland. The voice acting in Superliminal is also incredibly soulless. The performances lack any real emotion or personality, making it hard to connect with the game on any level. Comparing this to the voice acting in Portal, especially GLaDOS, it's clear how far Superliminal falls short. GLaDOS is a masterclass in voice acting, the same as Wheatley. Superliminal's voice acting, on the other hand, feels flat and uninspired. The storytelling is nowhere close to the quality of something like The Stanley Parable or Portal, which makes it interesting for me to see how this game is told to be a mixture of those. Comparing Superliminal to Portal or The Stanley Parable is an insult to those amazing pieces of work.

The last 30 minutes of the game were incredibly tiresome for me. Which is 25% of the game by the way. It felt like the designers ran out of clever puzzle ideas and just turned the game into a walking simulator. This part of the game dragged on and made me lose any remaining interest I had.

In conclusion, Superliminal is an insanely overrated and badly designed puzzle game. A good puzzle game should have variety, challenge, and creativity. Each puzzle should feel fresh and make you think in new ways. The solutions should be satisfying, making you feel smart for figuring them out. Superliminal doesn't do any of this. It's boring, overly simple, extremely repetitive, and falls highly short of its potential. If you’re looking for a good puzzle game, I’d recommend looking elsewhere. Superliminal simply doesn’t live up to the hype and is highly overrated.  It's simply, the very opposite of fun.

Actual review:

The game is a bit too short for it's price (there's an achievement for beating it under 30 minutes, possible without speedrunning expertise), and the puzzles are really not that hard. It isn't comparable to Portal 2 in puzzles nor story. If you're looking for a challenging puzzler, this is not it (unless you maybe find some good levels on the workshop).

On the other hand, it has a really odd vibe to it that I just absolutely love. The size thing is really mind-screwy, and it works well (they put in a lot of effort to make it work seamlessly). The achievements are also pretty fun and easy to get, and allow you to squeeze a few more hours out of the game.

The odd vibe thing also continues in the game's style and environments, which I absolutely love. The levels are quite surreal and you can really appreciate them if you take it all in, especially near the end.

This may not be for everyone, especially not for the 16€ for a couple hours of "new" gameplay, but if the game sticks with you, it's an unforgettable experience, and it's pretty fun to make your own levels.
Absolutely beautiful and well crafted game. It's short, but well worth $20 for the experience.  I really want to see a VR equivalent to this now.
